roles.statement: Founder, binding: every rule applies to exactly one role as its source and exactly one role or concrete surface as its target. No unions, no `any`, no `except`, no `/` between roles. The six roles are peers — each is a top-level folder holding packages (`layers/`, `framework/`, `applications/`, `tools/`, `deploy/`), with `service` being a package nested inside a layer.
roles.ruling12: A rule states the END STATE; enforcement level is a separate dial. No rule category may encode `mid-migration` — that turns a temporary mess into permanent vocabulary and excuses the migration from finishing. Three categories were deleted under this: `db:table (owner moved)`, `db:table (unowned, legacy)` and `db:table (unowned, never assigned)`. What is left is two table cells plus a completeness rule reported as a finding.
roles.kinds: single too — no `import+manifest`, no `all 8 kinds`. Eight kinds: import, manifest, di, api, mcp, event, table, capability.
roles.oneOffTarget: `development file` is the only target that is not a role or a package surface. It is the other axis entirely — file kind — and it belongs to the one rule the lint enforces, which is about file kind and nothing else.
roles.deployment: `deploy/` (chart, homebrew, bin) holds no package.json and no TypeScript, so it needs a synthetic actor or its files fall silently to the repo root. It has zero crossings in either direction today; its rows exist so the grid is complete.

structure.general: the rule is stated over a ROLE. Expanded, never merged: a rule that applies to four roles is four rows, each counting only its own instances. The count on a general row is the full aggregate for that one role.
structure.named: the rule names a specific package. It exists ONLY where the role-level row cannot carry the verdict; each named row states, in one sentence (`evidence`), the rule that is true of it and not of its role peers. Its instances are EXCLUDED from the general row it qualifies (`qualifies`).
structure.ordering: general rows first, in matrix order; named rows after, grouped by matrix and under the general row each one qualifies.
structure.pairs: `pairs` replaces per-package rows entirely. It lists every concrete (source → target) the row covers with prod/dev counts and the table owner inline — the inventory folded INSIDE the rule instead of duplicated beside it. `pairsTotal` is the true number of distinct pairs; `pairsShown` says how many are listed.
structure.completeness: Every role pair is generated. A cell earns a row when it is ALLOWED (so the permission list is complete, unused permissions included), when it has a live instance, when it is the enforced rule, or when a named row carves out of it. The rest are the default and are listed by name in `collapsedCells`.

defaults.principle: Every role pair is generated, then a cell earns a row only if it is ALLOWED (the permission list stays complete, unused permissions included), has a live instance, is the enforced rule, or is carved out by a named row. The rest are the default — forbidden, or unruled, with nothing in them — and are listed here by name with their rule text. Zero instances is the collapse condition, so no count moves.

findings: THE TABLE RULE IS TWO CELLS NOW (Ruling 12.2), and under it production access to a table owned by ANOTHER service is 1. Every production table access is by the owning service (421) or to one of the 6 tables that have no owner (90). The remaining problem is COMPLETENESS, not foreign reads.

`db:table (owner moved)` is gone. It was never a real category — the recovered registry records pre-AU26 `packages/…` paths and AU26 relocated five services. All five resolve to a current owner with exactly one production accessor, and forbidding them would have stopped `filesystems` reading the `filesystems` table.
ZERO production files import a development file (the four `→ development file` rows are live and at 0). Ruling 8.1 costs nothing to adopt and is pure regression protection.

`application → layer [api]` is LIVE, not empty — the previous census could not see it. `applications/remote-worker` is a detached process and dials both Layers with a raw `fetch` and a raw WebSocket; the detector now reads route registrations out of each Layer by AST and matches the dialled path longest-prefix-first, which is what distinguishes core-api's `/ws` from agent-orchestration's `/ws/worker`.

The two event rows that read like access rules were counting artefacts and are gone. `EventBus` is anonymous pub/sub, so every event site is a crossing with the bus and nothing else. What remains is one real breach: `framework → EventBus`, the single wildcard subscriber in `shared` — a good design in the wrong package, and the reason every emit in the repo used to attribute to `shared`.

`db:zod-schemas` no longer exists as a separately-ruled surface. Every symbol in it is `createSelectSchema(<one table>)`, so it inherits the table ACL symbol-by-symbol; allowing the barrel while forbidding the table import was a hole. The one production consumer now shows up as what it is: a layer root reading a schema generated from a table another service owns.

Four production `layer → framework [di]` instances were detector noise — frozen arrays from `shared` passed inline to `z.enum`. The DI detector no longer scores an imported constant as an injected port; 26 such arguments are now excluded repo-wide.

`db:util` should not exist: `escapeLikePattern`, `resolveAgentScaffoldSpecs` and `resolveProfile` touch no database. Kept as a surface only because the files are still in `db`; Ruling 12.3 makes the move a follow-up.
